newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Solidarity launches into nationwide protest.
newsitem.headline: Polish Solidarity launches into nationwide protest.

text.p: The Solidarity trade union plunged on Wednesday into Poland-wide protests to defend the Gdansk shipyard and other failing firms, holding furious demonstrations in the northern port city and occupying three Warsaw ministries.

"Today workers from Gdansk and Upper Silesia began a picket in the ministries of the Treasury, Finance and Economy," Solidarity spokesman Piotr Zak told Reuters. "In Gdansk, shipyard workers are blocking the offices of a parliamentary deputy from the (ruling, ex-communist) Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and we are also starting pickets of provincial government buildings," Zak said.

About 2,000 workers of the Gdansk yard, which is facing liquidation, bricked up the door to the deputy's office, wrote "Commies out of Poland" and hung up a red-painted pig's head in rage over the government's failure to save their jobs. The union's regional chiefs were meeting in Warsaw to decide on ways to escalate pressure on a government led by ex-communists who, in the case of troubled industries where Solidarity is strong, are now hard-nosed market reformers.
Witnesses said dozens of miners from the southern Silesia region where coal mines are struggling moved into key rooms of the Treasury ministry in Warsaw and brought in sleeping bags.

Gdansk workers have been demonstrating since the bankrupt yard's receiver announced earlier this month he would dismiss its last 3,800 employees and sell the assets piecemeal. The receiver acted after banks refused $100 million in credit to finance construction of five ships for a German shipowner, which could have kept the yard going.
The government did not encourage these credits, arguing that the ship contracts were deeply unsatisfactory.
But Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz on Tuesday met chiefs of Poland's merchant navy firm PZM and the successful Szczecin shipyard to find ways to save some of the Gdansk jobs.
His spokeswoman declined to reveal the outcome and said Cimoszewicz would inform parliament on Thursday.
Gdansk radio reported that the Szczecin yard may build ships in Gdansk for the Polska Zegluga Morska (PZM) company.
Although the central issue of the open-ended protest announced on Tuesday is the Gdansk shipyard where Solidarity emerged to defy communist rule in 1980, the issues are wider.
Solidarity Silesia region chief Marek Kempski said the issue was not just about a key symbol of Solidarity and employment in Gdansk, but also about jobs in mining.

"Several tens of mines...are in the same situation as the Gdansk shipyard today. The problem is 40 or 50 times greater (than just Gdansk)," he told public radio in an interview. He repeated that the union did not plan a general strike yet, but did not rule one out either.
"If...escalation of the protests yields nothing, a general strike is not out of the question," he said.

The fate of the enterprise which came to symbolise the democracy struggle leading to the 1989 fall of communism is arousing strong emotions and serving to rally opposition forces before parliamentary elections due around September this year. The union has steered dozens of small right-leaning groups into a Solidarity Election Action (AWS) which is now running about level in opinion polls with the ex-communist SLD, which has held power in coalition with a smaller Peasant party since 1993.
